claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is an as-solidified, single-phase solid solution.
Removing Co alters the local lattice distortion of FeNiCrMn relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Removing Co alters the intrinsic stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrMn.
Stacking-fault energy in the Co-free alloy varies with temperature and strain rate.
Changes in stacking-fault energy modify dislocation nucleation.
Changes in stacking-fault energy modify dislocation core structures and active slip systems.
Co removal shifts the balance between dislocation glide, cross-slip, and dynamic recovery.
At lower temperatures and strain rates, a higher effective stacking-fault energy may favor conventional glide and early recovery.
At higher temperatures and/or strain rates, reduced resistance to cross-slip modifies dislocation interactions and preserves ductility without undue strength loss.
The temperature- and strain-rate-dependent dislocation mechanisms govern shifts in the alloy's strength–ductility balance.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will show increased strain-rate sensitivity.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will show delayed dynamic recovery at elevated temperatures.
The Co-free alloy will exhibit a distinct temperature- and strain-rate-dependent strength–ductility profile relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies only to as-solidified, single-phase alloys having similar grain sizes and microstructural homogeneity.
Secondary-phase precipitation or substantial deviations in initial microstructure may invalidate the predicted behavior.
The alloys should be compared under identical processing, temperature, and strain-rate conditions.
A lack of statistically significant differences in stacking-fault-energy-related dislocation activity and dynamic-recovery onset would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism associates reduced resistance to cross-slip at higher temperature and/or strain rate with easier dislocation rearrangement, whereas the predicted outcome specifies delayed dynamic recovery at elevated temperature. Because cross-slip commonly enables recovery, the hypothesis does not explain how easier cross-slip produces delayed rather than accelerated recovery.
